title: Flatness and cartesianness from the square-zero ideal map
statement: Use algebraic spaces over a scheme $S$ and their small etale sites and structure sheaves [def-trf-algebraic-space, def-pc-scheme], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. A first order thickening $Z\hookrightarrow Z\prime$ means a representable closed immersion whose ideal sheaf has square zero and whose underlying closed subset is all of $Z\prime$; closed immersion is tested after every scheme base change, closed immersions of schemes being [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Module sheaves and quasi-coherence are [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category, def-trf-space-quasi-coherent-module]. Sheaf tensor products are [def-pur-sheaf-tensor-product]. Let $(f,f\prime):(Z\subset Z\prime)\to(Y\subset Y\prime)$ be a commutative square of first order thickenings over $S$. Let $\mathcal J_Y$ and $\mathcal J_Z$ be the respective ideal sheaves, regarded as modules on $Y$ and $Z$ on the common etale sites. Put $f^*\mathcal J_Y=\mathcal O_Z\otimes_{f^{-1}\mathcal O_Y}f^{-1}\mathcal J_Y$. If $f$ is flat (flatness on etale scheme charts [def-weil-flat-morphism]), the following are equivalent: $f\prime$ is flat and $Z\cong Y\times_{Y\prime}Z\prime$ via the given square; the canonical map $f^*\mathcal J_Y\to\mathcal J_Z$ is an isomorphism. Fibre products are the sheaf fibre products [lem-trf-space-fibre-products-etale-covers].

proof.text: At each geometric point $\bar z$ of $Z$, apply [lem-sfb-space-stalk-ideal-pullback] to obtain $A\prime\to B\prime$, quotients $A=A\prime/I$, $B=B\prime/J$, and the ideal-map stalk $q:I\otimes_A B\to J$. Both ideals have square zero. By [lem-sfb-space-strict-local-flatness], the assumed flatness of $f$ says that $B$ is flat over $A$ at every such point; flatness of $f\prime$ is equivalent to flatness of every $B\prime$ over $A\prime$. The stalk-calculus node also detects the sheaf isomorphism and identifies the cartesian condition with $J=IB\prime$ everywhere. Thus it remains to prove the two implications for these rings.

source.place: 06BH, lemma-deform, reduction to scheme charts; expressed in geometric stalks.

proof.text: Assume $f\prime$ is flat and the square is cartesian. At the fixed stalk $J=IB\prime$. Apply [lem-trf-flat-tensor-preserves-injection] to the inclusion $I\hookrightarrow A\prime$ and the flat $A\prime$-module $B\prime$. Using tensor symmetry and $A\prime\otimes_{A\prime}B\prime=B\prime$, its conclusion makes multiplication $I\otimes_{A\prime}B\prime\to B\prime$ injective, with image $IB\prime=J$. Because $I^2=0$, the module $I$ is an $A$-module. Clause (2) of [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-over-quotient-ring] identifies its source with $I\otimes_A(B\prime/IB\prime)=I\otimes_A B$. The multiplication is precisely $q$, so $q$ is bijective. This holds at every geometric point, hence the original ideal map is an isomorphism by [lem-sfb-space-stalk-ideal-pullback].

Conversely suppose the ideal map is an isomorphism. Its stalk $q$ is surjective by [lem-sfb-space-stalk-ideal-pullback]. Its image in $B\prime$ is exactly $IB\prime$: every image $q(i\otimes b)$ is the product of the image of $i$ and a lift of $b$, and each product $f\prime{}^\sharp(i)b\prime$ is $q(i\otimes\bar b\prime)$. Finite sums give both inclusions, so $J=IB\prime$. The value is independent of the lift since $f\prime{}^\sharp(I)\subseteq J$ and $J^2=0$. This equality at all stalks proves that the given square is cartesian by the same stalk-calculus node.

With $J=IB\prime$, clause (2) of [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-over-quotient-ring] gives $I\otimes_{A\prime}B\prime\cong I\otimes_A B$. Under this isomorphism multiplication into $B\prime$ factors as the bijection $q$ followed by the inclusion $J\hookrightarrow B\prime$, hence is injective. Moreover $B\prime/IB\prime=B$ is flat over $A\prime/I=A$ by Step 1. Apply [lem-sfb-nilpotent-ideal-module-flatness] with $R=A\prime$, $M=B\prime$ and $n=2$ to deduce that $B\prime$ is flat over $A\prime$. This at every geometric point implies that $f\prime$ is flat by [lem-sfb-space-strict-local-flatness]. Together with Step 3 it proves the converse.
